The Lord, Blessed and Exalted, says: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: ﴿By the star when it sets, your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [An-Najm 1, 2]. "An-najm" (the star) is a generic noun, meant to include all the stars. His saying ﴿when it sets﴾ has two meanings. The first meaning: when it sets (disappears). The second meaning: ﴿when it sets﴾, that is, when a shooting star falls from it upon the devils who eavesdrop. ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ is the answer to the oath. The answer to the oath, that is, the thing sworn to, is ﴿your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾. ﴿Has not strayed﴾ means he was not ignorant. ﴿Nor has he erred﴾ means he did not act out of obstinate deviation. This is because opposing the truth is either due to ignorance or due to deliberate deviation. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become clear from the wrong﴾ [Al-Baqarah 256]. So when ignorance is negated from the Prophet ﷺ, and deliberate deviation is negated from him, it becomes clear that his method (ﷺ) is knowledge and right guidance. Knowledge is the opposite of ignorance, which is straying: ﴿has not strayed﴾. Right guidance is the opposite of deviation: ﴿the right course has become clear from the wrong﴾.

Therefore, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, his speech is true and his law is true, because it stems from knowledge and right guidance. His saying ﴿your companion has not strayed﴾ addresses the Quraysh. He described him with this attribute to indicate that they know him, know his lineage, know his truthfulness and know his trustworthiness. He was not a stranger to them, such that they could say, "We do not believe in him because we do not know him." Rather, he was their companion who grew up among them. This is one point.

Second: since he is their companion, the requirement of companionship is that they should believe him and support him, not that they should be his enemies. So in his saying ﴿your companion﴾, there are, then, two benefits. The first benefit: he is their companion whom they know; he is not unknown among them, nor a stranger to them. So how is it that yesterday they described him as "the trustworthy," and now they describe him as "the liar, the traitor"?

The second benefit: the requirement of companionship is that they should believe him and support him, not that they should oppose him. That is to say, he did not say, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has not strayed," or "Muhammad has not strayed." Rather, ﴿your companion has not strayed﴾. So the benefit of this is what we have mentioned to you: that the requirement of companionship is that they should be people who know him, and the requirement of companionship is that they should be people who support him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 3:

﴿Nor does he speak from desire.﴾ [An-Najm: 3] That is: he does not speak anything that issues from desire in any circumstance. He does not rule on any matter out of desire; rather, he speaks only what has been revealed to him of the Qur'an, and what has been revealed to him of the Sunnah, and what he (ﷺ) exercised ijtihad (independent reasoning) in, seeking thereby the public good. Thus his speech (ﷺ) consists of three categories.

The first: that he speaks the Qur'an.

The second: that he speaks the revealed Sunnah, which Allah the Exalted approved upon his tongue.

The third: that he speaks by ijtihad (independent reasoning), intending thereby only the public good.

We speak about what we intend as good, and we also speak from desire. Is every one of us free from desire? No. A person inclines toward his companion, inclines toward his relative, inclines toward the rich, inclines toward the poor. But the Prophet (ﷺ) cannot speak from desire.

Since he cannot speak from desire, he speaks only the truth: if it is from the Qur'an, then it is the Qur'an; if it is from the revealed Sunnah, then it is the Sunnah; and if it is from the Sunnah derived through ijtihad, then in every case he is rewarded.

Then He said: ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [An-Najm 4]. Meaning: the Noble Quran is nothing but a revelation revealed, that is, a revelation from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Who is the intermediary between Allah and the Messenger? ﴿He has taught him one mighty in power﴾ [An-Najm 5]. Meaning: the one mighty in power taught the Prophet ﷺ this revelation. ﴿Mighty in power﴾, that is, one possessing great strength, and this is Jibril (peace be upon him), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [possessing] power, with the Lord of the Throne secure [in position]﴾ [At-Takwir 19–20]. So Jibril (peace be upon him) is strong, mighty, trustworthy and noble; it is absolutely impossible for him to fall short in conveying this revelation which he brought to Muhammad (ﷺ), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be of the warners﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 193–194].

﴿He has taught him one mighty in power﴾: ﴿Mighty in power﴾ means: possessor of great powers, so it is an idafah of the attribute to the thing it describes.

﴿Mighty in power (5), possessor of vigor﴾ [An-Najm 5–6]. ﴿Mighty in power﴾ means: he is strong, and al-mirrah (vigor) means: a good form, so he is possessed of strength and of beauty and goodliness.

The Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in his original form which he was created upon, having six hundred wings which filled the horizon. He is the one who brought down this Quran until he cast it upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be of the warners (194), in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 193–195].

And His saying: ﴿then He rose (istawa)﴾ [Al-Fath 29]: meaning, He acted, or He completed; for istiwa' in the Arabic language is sometimes mentioned unrestricted, so its meaning is completion. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown (istawa), We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Al-Qasas 14], meaning: he became complete.

And sometimes it is restricted by (ʿalā), so its meaning is elevation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride (12), that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you have settled (istawaytum) upon them﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12–13]. He said: ﴿that you may sit upon their backs﴾ and said: ﴿when you have settled upon them﴾, meaning: you have risen upon them (ʿalawtum ʿalayhi).

From it is His saying, Exalted is He, in describing Himself: ﴿The Most Merciful, above the Throne, istawa﴾ [Ta-Ha 5], meaning: He is elevated above it, Mighty and Majestic. The elevation is specific to the Throne, and this is other than the absolute elevation over all created things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 7:

Then he drew near and came down (close), (Q. 53:8) [He drew near to the Prophet ﷺ], and "came down" means he approached from above. So he was (Q. 53:9) "at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer," and this is a figure of speech used for closeness. "Qāba qawsayn" means very, very close, "or nearer," where "aw" (or) carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), that is, he was even nearer than that.

Then he drew near and came down (close), (Q. 53:8) [He drew near to the Prophet ﷺ], and "came down" means he approached from above. So he was (Q. 53:9) "at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer," and this is a figure of speech used for closeness. "Qāba qawsayn" means very, very close, "or nearer," where "aw" (or) carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), that is, he was even nearer than that.

ﻓَﺄَوْحَى ﴿So He revealed﴾ [An-Najm 10], i.e., Jibril (Gabriel) revealed ﴿to His servant what He revealed﴾ [An-Najm 10], i.e., to the servant of Allah. The pronoun in "awha" (He revealed) refers to Jibril, and the pronoun in "ʿabdihi" (His servant) refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; meaning, Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah "mā awḥā" (what he revealed).

He did not specify what was revealed, as a means of glorifying it, because vagueness (ibhām) is used to convey grandeur and magnificence. Among its examples is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Ṭāhā 78], meaning: there covered them something great.

Here, ﴿He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ means: of a great matter. And there is no speech greater than the Noble Qur'an, since it is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 11:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [An-Najm 11], concerning the story of the Mi'raj (the Ascension).

Know, O Muslim brother, that the Prophet ﷺ had an Isra' (the Night Journey) and a Mi'raj (the Ascension). The Isra' is mentioned by Allah in Surah al-Isra', and the Mi'raj is mentioned by Allah in Surah an-Najm. Both took place in one night, before the Hijrah by about three years or a year and a half; historians have differed on this. Furthermore, the Isra' and the Mi'raj occurred with the body of the Prophet ﷺ and his soul, not with his soul alone.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ [Al-Isra' 60], the intended meaning is a sight seen with the eye, not a dream seen in sleep.

Allah, exalted is He, says in the context of the verses about the Mi'raj: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [An-Najm 11]. ﴿Al-fu'ad﴾ means the heart. The meaning is that what the Prophet ﷺ saw with his eye, he also saw with his heart, affirmed and knew with certainty. This is because the eye may see something and the heart may deny it, and the heart may perceive something and the eye may deny it. For example, a person may see a figure with his eye and think it is so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, but the heart refuses this, because he knows that so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, was not in this place. Here the eye saw and the heart denied, or the reverse: a person may imagine something in his heart, but the eye denies it.

As for what the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) saw on the night of the Mi'raj, he saw it truly, with his sight and his insight. For this reason He said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [An-Najm 11]. Rather, the heart agreed with what the eye saw. The Prophet ﷺ was not lying about the great signs he saw that night; rather, he was truthful. But you know that the polytheists denied him, and said: "How can he reach Bayt al-Maqdis and ascend to the heavens in one night?!"

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 12:

So He said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [An-Najm 12]. The interrogative here is for denial and astonishment. The meaning of "tumaruna" (tumārūnahu) is: you argue with him with the intent of prevailing over him. For this reason it is followed by "ʿalā" (on) rather than "fī" (in). That is, He did not say "afatumārūnahu fīmā yarā" (will you dispute with him about what he sees), but said ﴿over what he sees﴾, indicating that the verb has taken on the sense of contending for victory. That is: will you argue with him, wishing to overcome him, ﴿over what he sees﴾, meaning over something he saw. However, He expressed what was seen in the past with the present tense (yarā), indicating the bringing-to-presence of this thing, and that when he, upon him be blessings and peace, reported it, it was as if he were seeing it now. This is because when a person speaks of something past, someone may say: "Perhaps he forgot and erred." But when it is expressed in the present tense, it becomes as if he is speaking of something he is witnessing.

﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees﴾: does the meaning refer to what he sees now, or to what he saw before, but expressed what he saw before in the present tense?

Second: Pay attention to this great subtlety (nukta), by which I mean: the profound wisdom, where the expressions of the Noble Qur'an, when they are phrased contrary to what is expected, there must be a wisdom that becomes apparent to the one who reflects.

(رآه) The subject (al-fa'il) is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the object (al-maf'ul bihi) is Jibril (Gabriel). That is, Muhammad saw Jibril. ﴿نَزْلَةً أُخْرَى﴾ means "another time," i.e., a second time, when he descended.

So what was the first time? The first time, the Messenger (ﷺ) saw Jibril while he was in the Cave of Hira', he saw him in his original form. Do you know how he saw him? He saw him with six hundred wings, having filled the horizon. This shows his greatness: the whole horizon around the Messenger (ﷺ) in Hira' was filled by the wings of this noble angel. For this reason Allah described him as ﴿ذِي قُوَّةٍ عِنْدَ ذِي الْعَرْشِ مَكِينٍ﴾ [At-Takwir 20], "possessing strength, held in high station with the Lord of the Throne," and as one of ﴿ذُو مِرَّةٍ﴾, that is, of good form, as has already been mentioned in this surah. So he saw him once on the earth and once at the horizon of the heaven.

Where on the earth? He was in the Cave of Hira'. As for in the heaven, it was above the heavens. Sometimes he saw him from beneath the heaven, from above the earth, and sometimes from above the heaven. For this reason He said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ رَآهُ نَزْلَةً أُخْرَى﴾, "nazlatan" meaning "another time."

"Near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary" [An-Najm 53:14]. He saw him near the Lote-tree. The lote-tree is well known on earth as the sidr tree, but the lote-tree that is in the seventh heaven is not like the lote-tree of this world: its fruit is like the large jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. It is a great tree, and it was named the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary because every thing that ascends from the earth ends at it, and every thing that descends from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ends at it. So it is a boundary from both sides. The first side: what ascends from the earth to the heaven ends at this lote-tree; what descends from the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, ends with this lote-tree; and what ascends from the earth also ends at it. So it is a boundary from both sides.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 15:

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [An-Najm: 15]. So: the Garden is above the seventh heaven. Since the Lote-tree (sidrah) is above the seventh heaven, and the Garden is near it, what follows? It follows that the Garden is above the seventh heaven, and so it is. Its highest and middle part is al-Firdaws (may Allah make us and you among its people), above which is the Throne of the Most Merciful, exalted is He. For this reason Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿No indeed! The record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 18], and ʿIlliyyūn is an intensive form of height; meaning: the highest of all things. The main point is that Allah says: ﴿near it﴾, i.e., near this Lote-tree, ﴿is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [An-Najm: 15]. Al-Ma'wa means the final destination. And whose refuge? The refuge of those who combined faith with righteous deeds. It is their abode, they take refuge in it and abide in it forever. As for the Fire, it is the abode of the disbelievers, and we seek refuge with Allah.

In this there is clear evidence that the ultimate destination of all creation, jinn and humans alike, is either the Garden or the Fire, and there is no third. So jinn and humans are either in the Fire or in the Garden. Al-Safarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his creed:

"Every human and every jinn, in the abode of Fire or the bliss of the Garden."

There is no other abode besides these. Are graves a mathwa (abode) and a ma'wa (refuge)? No, they are not an abode, not even for the dead, because the graves are a passage and a crossing, since behind the graves is resurrection.

It is related that a Bedouin Arab heard a reciter recite the words of Allah the Most High: ﴿Your competition for more distracts you, until you visit the graves﴾ [At-Takathur: 1-2]. The Bedouin said, by his natural disposition and his Arabic: "By Allah, the visitor does not remain, and indeed there is something beyond that."

What is meant by "the visitor does not remain"? The visitor visits and then moves on. Likewise, people stay in the graves as long as Allah wills them to stay, and then they come out of them. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 100]. So people will certainly be resurrected.

The expression we sometimes hear or read, that "they carried the man to his final abode," meaning the cemetery, is an incorrect expression. Why? Because graves are not the final abode. And if the one who says it believed its meaning, it would necessarily follow that he denies resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 16:

﴿When the Lote-tree was covered by that which covered it.﴾ [an-Najm: 16] Which Lote-tree is meant? It is the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), because He said earlier: ﴿And he saw him another time, by the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [an-Najm: 13-14], and then said: ﴿When the Lote-tree was covered﴾ [an-Najm: 16]. The definite article (al) in such an expression is called by the grammarians al lil-'ahd al-dhikri (the "al" of prior mention), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger. But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15-16].

﴿When the Lote-tree was covered﴾ [an-Najm: 16], meaning: the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. ﴿by that which covered it﴾ [an-Najm: 16]: Allah left that undefined for magnification and exaltation; meaning, something mighty covered it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There covered it of beauty and splendour what no one can describe."[[Muslim (162/259) narrated from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was brought the Buraq, a white animal, long, above the donkey and below the mule, placing its hoof at the farthest point of its sight," and in it: "When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah, it changed, and no one among the creation of Allah is able to describe its beauty," the hadith.]] Glory be to Allah, the Mighty. ﴿When the Lote-tree was covered by that which covered it﴾. Similar to this in leaving things undefined for magnification is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Then the sea covered them with what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78], meaning: the water of the sea covered them with what covered them, and it was something great. Likewise here: ﴿When the Lote-tree was covered by that which covered it﴾, meaning: something great covered it by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in an instant, "Be," and it is.

The Qur'an verse 53:17 is in ﴿ ﴾ markers. Translating faithfully.

﴿The eye did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ [An-Najm 17]

Whose eye? The eye of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Nor did it transgress.﴾ The scholars say: "Zaagh" means it deviated to the right and left; "taghā" means it went beyond what was in front of it. That is, the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) was at the height of courtesy (adab) in this great station. He did not turn his gaze right and left, nor did his sight extend beyond what he was permitted to look at. This was from the perfection of his courtesy (peace and blessings be upon him). It is the custom that when a person enters a strange house, you find him looking right and left, wondering what this house is like. Especially when a great change takes place in that very moment, one must look to see what has happened. But because of the perfection of the Prophet's courtesy (ﷺ), his steadfastness of heart, and his bearing of what no other human being could bear, he attained this great courtesy, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾ whose eye? The Messenger's (ﷺ); that is, it did not deviate to the right or left; it did not turn to the right or left. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾, it did not go beyond what was in front of it. Rather, he was at the utmost perfection of courtesy (peace and blessings be upon him). For this reason Allah said of him: ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ [Al-Qalam 4]

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [An-Najm 18]. Who saw? The Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed he saw﴾ — and you, my Muslim brother who recites the Qur'an, will always encounter such an expression: ﴿Indeed he saw﴾, ﴿Indeed We created man in toil﴾ [Al-Balad 4], ﴿And indeed We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 12], and so on; there are many examples. The scholars say that this sentence is emphasized with three kinds of emphasis: the first: an implied oath; the second: the lam; and the third: qad. This is because the meaning of (wa-laqad) is: "By Allah, indeed," so the sentence is emphasized by the oath, the lam, and qad. The oath is implied, but the context indicates it.

﴿Saw﴾ means: the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [An-Najm 18]. The āyah (sign) is the indicator specific to what it signifies, which no one else shares; otherwise it would not be a sign, i.e., it would not be an āyah. So an āyah must be specific to what it signifies. Not every indicator is an āyah; rather, it is the one that is specific to what it signifies.

What the Prophet (peace be upon him) saw of the signs of Allah is great and magnificent. As for His saying ﴿al-kubrā (the greatest)﴾: it has been said that it is a second object of (raʾā) ﴿Indeed he saw of the signs of his Lord﴾, the āyah ﴿the greatest﴾ [An-Najm 18].

It has also been said that al-kubrā is an adjective of āyāt, and the meaning is: he saw of the great signs of Allah. The second view is more correct and closer; that is, he saw of the greatest signs what he saw, and what he saw is not the greatest thing, for there may be something greater that we do not know.

The conclusion: the Messenger saw in this Mi'raj of the great signs of Allah what he had not seen before, and what no human could endure patiently. If we saw the great pavilion of a king, we would be dazzled and amazed and would begin looking right and left. But the Messenger (peace be upon him) did not have his mind or his composure altered; rather he was in the most complete state of composure. Otherwise, he was carried by night from the Sacred Mosque — from al-Hijr beside the Ka'bah, and al-Hijr is part of the Ka'bah — he was carried from that place to Bayt al-Maqdis, a journey of a month or two months? Two months, in a moment; because he rode al-Buraq, and al-Buraq is a great, strong, swift animal whose stride reaches as far as its sight, and it is very swift. He arrived there and prayed with the prophets. Then he was taken up to the heavens. And how far is the heaven from the earth? Very far. Then from heaven to heaven, and the angels met him and asked: they said to Jibril: "Who is with you?" He said: "Muhammad." They said: "Has he been sent for?" He said: "Yes." Then he greeted some of the prophets in the heavens. Then prayer was enjoined upon him, and he went back and forth between Allah and Musa. All of this while he, peace be upon him, remained steadfast in heart. This was a real matter: he himself, peace be upon him, ascended. For this reason, when he came and told the people the next day, Quraysh denied it, because they deny what cannot be conceived by their minds. Denying what cannot be conceived by the mind is not limited to the disbelievers of Quraysh; even among those who ascribe themselves to this Ummah, some have denied attributes of Allah that He affirmed for Himself, because on their claim they cannot be conceived by the mind. Is that not so? There are people who ascribe themselves to the Islamic Ummah and are of its people, who have denied some of the attributes of Allah which He affirmed for Himself, because according to their claim they are not conceivable to the mind.

Quraysh denied this Mi'raj. Tell me: if it had been a dream, would Quraysh have denied it? They would not, because dreams can contain such things. But it was a real, sensory matter: the Messenger (peace be upon him) was taken by night in his body and ascended in one night, all these things happened, and then he returned to the earth and prayed the Fajr prayer in Makkah (peace be upon him).

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. This indicates that the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, include the great and what is less than that; we do not say "and among them the small." This is because al-kubrā is a superlative form (ism tafdil), and the one who erred among the later exegetes, who said that al-kubrā is an active participle (ism fa'il), is mistaken; rather it is a superlative, because the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are either great, or greatest and most magnificent. The Mi'raj that occurred is without doubt among the greatest and magnificent signs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verses 19–20:

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned what the Prophet (ﷺ) had seen of the great signs of his Lord on the horizons, He said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ This interrogative is for belittling and debasing, meaning: the lowliness of the rank of these idols which Allah, mighty and majestic, has mentioned. That is, tell me, after you have heard the great signs of Allah that you have heard, tell me about the matter of these idols: what is their worth, what is their standing, what is their honour?

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza? (19) And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [An-Najm 19–20] These are three well-known idols among the Arabs, whom they worship besides Allah. They submit to them as they submit to Allah, and they draw near to them as they draw near to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Yet they believe that these idols will not benefit them in times of hardship: when they board ships and call upon Allah, sincerely devoting their religion to Him, they know that none will deliver them from this hardship except the Lord of the worlds. But Satan embellished for them and gave them false hopes regarding the worship of these idols, which they claim bring them closer to Allah, the Exalted, as Allah said about them: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [Az-Zumar 3]. But in reality they do not bring them near to Allah; rather they distance them from Him.

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza? (19) And Manat, the third﴾ [An-Najm 19–20]: "the third" is relative to the two before it, and "the other" means the one that comes last. It seems, and Allah knows best, that among the Arabs Manat was of lower rank than al-Lat and al-'Uzza.

That is: "Do you attribute to yourselves the males and to Allah the females?!" This was in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, while they did not witness the creation of the angels and were not informed of that, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 19]. The answer is: No, they did not witness their creation. Yet this testimony will be recorded against them: ﴿Their testimony will be written down, and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 19]. We ask Allah for well-being.

What do they do when one of them is given the good news of a female? ﴿His face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief. He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given good news of﴾ [An-Nahl 58, 59]. Yet despite this, they attribute to the Lord of the worlds, who created the male and the female, daughters, and they attribute to themselves sons. Is this division a just division or an unjust one? Listen to the answer: ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [An-Najm 22]. That is: that division, namely that they attribute daughters to Allah and sons to themselves, is ﴿an unfair division﴾, meaning unjust, deviating from the truth. For if we said it was permissible for Allah to have a child, it would be more fitting for Him to have sons, since sons are undoubtedly higher than daughters, and He, glorified and exalted, is higher than the created beings. So the higher must belong to the higher and the lower to the lower. This is the just division.

Then there is another division, lower than this in justice, but still containing some justice: that they attribute daughters to Allah and have daughters themselves, and attribute sons to Allah and have sons themselves. But they did not do this. They assigned the lower to the Creator and the higher to themselves. For this reason, the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [An-Najm 22].

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, returned to explain the reality of these worshipped idols, and said: ﴿They are nothing but names that you have named﴾ [An-Najm 23]. "In" (إِنْ) here is a negative particle meaning "not" (ما). This is a rule that the student of knowledge benefits from: when "illa" (إلا, "except") follows "in" and is affirmative, then "in" here is negative, as in: "in hadha illa basharun" (this is nothing but a human), "in hadha illa mujtahid" (this is nothing but a diligent person), and similar expressions.

So "in" here is negative, meaning: "They are nothing but names that you have named"; that is, these idols are nothing but mere names with no reality behind them. You named them gods, you named them worshipped beings, but there is no reality to that; they are only names. Does a name indicate what it names? No. If you named iron "wood," it would not become wood; if you named wood "iron," it would not become iron; if you named a mule "donkey," it would not be a donkey; and so on. These idols they call "gods"; will they actually be gods? No.

It is merely a name, and a name without a named reality has no benefit. Therefore He said: ﴿They are﴾, meaning: these idols and the things named, ﴿nothing but names that you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾. ﴿You﴾ refers to the addressees who lived to see the mission, and ﴿your fathers﴾ means the earlier forefathers. "Mere names" ﴿for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾: "ma" (مَا) here is negative, meaning that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has sent down no proof for them. Proof is called "sultan" (سُلْطَان, authority) because the one who possesses proof has an authority by which he prevails over his opponent; whoever has no proof has no authority. Thus "sultan" always means "hujjah" (proof), i.e., evidence, because whoever has the proof holds authority over his opponent.

Regarding ﴿in yattabi'una illa al-zann﴾ [An-Najm 23], what do you say about "in"? ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾: "in" is negative, meaning "not." Based on the rule I mentioned to you, that when "illa" comes affirmative after "in," then "in" is negative. ﴿They follow﴾, meaning these people and their fathers, ﴿nothing but conjecture﴾, meaning the illusion that has no reality; because they say, "These are gods," so on what did they rely? On illusion. Thus "zann" here means "wahm" (illusion); that is, those who say they are gods follow nothing but conjecture, i.e., illusion, imagination that has no reality. ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture, and what their souls desire﴾, meaning what their souls incline toward of falsehood.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And certainly there has come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾ [An-Najm 23]. The sentence here is emphasized with three emphatics: the implied oath, the lam, and "qad." This construction is frequent in the Noble Qur'an, and it is an emphasis with three emphatics, as I told you: the oath, the lam, and "qad." The oath is implied: "By Allah, indeed there has come to them from their Lord the guidance." The lam is present and "qad" is present, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, here affirms that guidance has indeed come to them from their Lord. In His saying ﴿from their Lord﴾ He did not say "from Allah," as an indication that the Sharia may only be received from Allah, because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Lord, and the Lord is the Creator, the Owner, the Governor.

﴿The guidance﴾ is the subject of "came," and what is meant by it is knowledge, in contrast to His saying ﴿they follow nothing but conjecture﴾: they follow conjecture, while knowledge has come from Allah. ﴿And certainly there has come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾, meaning knowledge upon the tongue of His messengers, peace be upon them, who were sealed by the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 53, verse 24–25:

﴿Or is it for man whatever he wishes?﴾ [An-Najm: 24]. Here, ﴿أم﴾ (am) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), because it comes in two forms: connected (muttasilah) and disjunctive (munqati'ah). When there is a counterpart, it is connected; when there is no counterpart, it is disjunctive. If you say, "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?", it is connected. But when it occurs in a verse like this one, ﴿Or is it for man whatever he wishes?﴾, it means "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. That is: "Rather, is it for man whatever he wishes?" The interrogation here is for denial and negation; that is, it is not for man whatever he wishes. A person may wish for many things, but they do not come to pass, because there is a Manager, who is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So it is not for man whatever he wishes. This points to something specific: it is a rebuttal of the conduct of these polytheists who worship idols, claiming that they bring them closer to Allah. Is that something they have?

The answer: They do not have that. Their idols do not bring them closer. It is also a rebuttal of their saying that the daughters belong to Allah and the sons belong to them. Do they have that? No. Even if they wish for this and it occurs in their imagination, it does not come to pass, because to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life. Hence He said: ﴿So to Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾ [An-Najm: 25]. ﴿And for man is not whatever he wishes.﴾ Often in daily life a person wishes for something but it does not happen; often a person wishes for a thing and strives for its causes but it does not happen, because the matter is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Hence He said: ﴿So to Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾, and He began with the Hereafter, because the dominion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, appears in the Hereafter more than in this world. In this world there are kings, presidents and leaders whom the common people see as having authority, but in the Hereafter this does not exist: ﴿The Day they will come out, nothing of them concealed from Allah. [It will be said], "Whose is the dominion today?" [It is] for Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. Thus said Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
